questions.stem: What is object detection in Computer Vision, and how is its output different from image classification and semantic segmentation?
options: Object detection finds several objects and gives a class to each, but draws a single box around the whole scene. Image classification estimates each object's position, while segmentation labels pixels.

Object detection names and locates each visible object with a bounding box and confidence score. Image classification labels the entire image, while semantic segmentation assigns categories to individual pixels.

Object detection finds objects and marks their exact pixels instead of reporting boxes. Classification gives a separate class to every detected object, while semantic segmentation predicts one label for the complete image.

Object detection names every object in an image and predicts a confidence score, but does not estimate location. Image classification predicts boxes for each instance, while segmentation identifies the class of individual pixels.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Object detection answers two questions: what objects are present, and where are they? A traffic image may contain several cars, each with its own box, class, and score. Image classification might simply label the whole image 'street scene.' Semantic segmentation labels pixels by category; instance segmentation can separate individual masks. Detection boxes approximate object extents rather than outlining every pixel. Applications include retail inventory, road safety, and industrial inspection.

questions.stem: How are bounding boxes, class labels, confidence scores, and coordinate formats represented in an object detection output?
options: A detection includes a class, score, and coordinates, but x1, y1, x2, y2 always means the box center and its size. Resizing changes the image but never changes the required pixel coordinates.

A detection includes a class label, box, and confidence score, but that score measures how much image area the object occupies. Coordinates may be normalized or pixel based without any conversion between them.

A detection includes a class label, score, and box coordinates, but confidence is always a calibrated probability of being right. Boxes can mix corner and center formats because the evaluation software automatically infers which convention was used.

A detection commonly includes a class label, confidence score, and box coordinates such as x1, y1, x2, y2. Coordinates must match the image scale and chosen format; resizing or cropping requires corresponding box transformations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A bounding box can use two opposite corners, (x1, y1, x2, y2), or its center, width and height. The illustrated detector reports a car with confidence 0.94 and a box from (155,137) to (428,232). Some systems use coordinates divided by image width and height. When a picture is resized, cropped, or flipped, change its boxes too. Confidence is a model score, not automatically a calibrated probability. Use one coordinate convention consistently through training and evaluation.
questions.technicalExplanation: A common box format is (x1, y1, x2, y2), where the points are opposite corners. Another format is (center x, center y, width, height); normalized coordinates use image-relative values. A detector might return 'dog', 0.92, and (20, 30, 130, 170). If the image is resized or flipped, the box must be transformed too. Confidence is a model score, not automatically a trustworthy probability. Training labels and evaluation predictions must follow matching coordinate conventions.

questions.stem: What does Intersection over Union (IoU) measure for bounding boxes, and why is it useful when matching predicted objects to ground truth?
options: IoU is shared box area divided by the total area covered by both boxes. It measures how well a predicted box fits the actual object, helping decide whether a detection counts as a match.
IoU measures the overlap area divided by the predicted box's area, regardless of the annotation's size. A box fully inside a much larger labeled object can therefore receive a perfect overlap score.

IoU measures the overlap between two boxes divided by the area of their smallest enclosing rectangle. It treats the empty corners within that rectangle as part of the union even when neither box covers them.
IoU measures how close the centers of two boxes are and converts that distance to a percentage. Two boxes can earn a high score whenever their centers match, even if their widths differ greatly.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Intersection over Union (IoU) measures how closely two bounding boxes overlap. Divide the intersection area by the union area. In the diagram, two 100×100 boxes are shifted 20 pixels horizontally. Their intersection is 80×100 = 8,000, and their union is 12,000, so IoU ≈ 0.667. During evaluation, an object is matched when the predicted class is right and IoU reaches the selected threshold. Confidence and duplicate suppression are checked separately.
questions.technicalExplanation: IoU equals intersection area divided by union area for two boxes. For two overlapping 50×50 boxes offset by five pixels in both directions, the overlap is 45×45 = 2,025 and the union is 2,975, giving IoU ≈ 0.681. Evaluators can match a detection to an unmatched ground-truth object when the class matches and IoU exceeds a chosen threshold. IoU judges localization; confidence scoring and duplicate handling remain separate concerns.

questions.stem: How do one-stage and two-stage object detectors differ, and what must happen to bounding-box labels when training images are augmented?
options: One-stage detectors generate region proposals first and classify those regions separately, whereas two-stage detectors predict boxes directly. Augmented images can keep the original boxes because only pixel appearance changes when the picture is flipped.

Both detector families require a proposal network, but one-stage detectors simply classify fewer proposals. Augmentation can modify the input photograph while leaving object coordinates unchanged whenever the class label itself remains the same.

One-stage detectors predict classes and boxes directly from image features. Two-stage detectors first generate proposals, then refine and classify them. During augmentation, box coordinates must change along with flips, crops, and scaling.

One-stage detectors predict boxes and classes directly, while two-stage models first create proposals for refinement. During cropping or flipping, the class labels may stay the same but the boxes should always keep their original positions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In a one-stage detector, a prediction head outputs candidate classes and boxes from features in one main detection pass. Two-stage systems such as Faster R-CNN generate region proposals and then classify or refine them. Real speed depends on architecture and hardware, not just the stage label. For augmentation, a horizontal flip must move each box horizontally; cropping may clip or remove boxes. Failing to update target coordinates teaches the detector incorrect locations.

questions.stem: How can Python compute IoU between two boxes and apply non-maximum suppression (NMS) to reduce duplicate object detections?
questions.tag: Medium · IoU and NMS in Python
options: Compute the overlap of two boxes and rank detections by confidence, then remove the highest-scoring box whenever its overlap exceeds the threshold. This leaves the weaker duplicate proposals and discards the strongest candidate first.

Calculate intersection and union areas for boxes in the same coordinate format, then divide them to get IoU. Apply NMS by confidence order, suppressing lower-scoring boxes with IoU above a chosen threshold.

Compute intersection over union by dividing the shared area by the smaller box's area, then remove predictions with the least overlap. This method treats well-separated objects as duplicates and keeps heavily overlapping proposals.

Calculate standard IoU for predicted boxes, but run suppression in the order the detections were generated rather than by confidence. A weaker duplicate may remain while the stronger box is removed, even if both identify the same object.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Non-maximum suppression addresses overlapping predictions for the same object. Sort detections by confidence, keep a strong prediction, and discard lower-scoring boxes that overlap it beyond a threshold. The example below uses three xyxy boxes: the first two overlap with IoU ≈ 0.681, while the third is separate. At NMS IoU threshold 0.5, indices 0 and 2 remain. Production detectors often apply class-aware NMS, score thresholds, and optimized library operators.

Python · IoU and simple greedy NMS 14 lines · one class
01 def iou(a, b):
02     x1, y1 = max(a[0],b[0]), max(a[1],b[1])
03     x2, y2 = min(a[2],b[2]), min(a[3],b[3])
04     overlap = max(0,x2-x1) * max(0,y2-y1)
05     area = lambda p: max(0,p[2]-p[0])*max(0,p[3]-p[1])
06     return overlap / max(area(a)+area(b)-overlap, 1e-9)
07 boxes = [(10,10,60,60),(15,15,65,65),(90,10,130,50)]
08 scores = [0.95,0.85,0.78]
09 kept = []
10 for idx in sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i:scores[i], reverse=True):
11     if all(iou(boxes[idx],boxes[j]) <= 0.5 for j in kept):
12         kept.append(idx)
13 print('IoU:', round(iou(boxes[0], boxes[1]), 3))
14 print('NMS kept:', kept)

Expected output: IoU 0.681 · NMS keeps indices [0, 2]. Run NMS per class when detections include different categories.

Rank boxes by confidence and remove highly overlapping lower-scoring duplicates. This example uses a 0.5 IoU suppression threshold.

questions.stem: How should engineers interpret AP, mAP, IoU thresholds, and per-class errors when evaluating object detection models?
options: Average Precision is the average confidence of boxes predicted for one class, while mAP averages those confidence values over classes. Changing IoU thresholds affects the geometry of boxes but not how precision and recall are calculated.

Average Precision counts correct bounding boxes but ignores false alarms and missing objects, while mAP averages the scores across image resolutions. IoU thresholds matter during training but are unnecessary when evaluating predicted versus annotated boxes.

Average Precision measures precision at one fixed confidence threshold without tracking the recall trade-off, while mAP reports the highest class score. A model's single overall mAP value replaces the need to investigate per-class errors.

Average Precision summarizes a class's precision-recall performance under a defined matching rule. Mean AP averages across classes; COCO's primary AP also averages IoU thresholds from 0.50 through 0.95, revealing stricter localization failures.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For object detection, precision and recall depend on matching predicted boxes to annotated objects at a specified IoU threshold and ranking detections by confidence. Average Precision (AP) summarizes the resulting precision-recall curve for a class. Mean AP (mAP) aggregates classes; the main COCO AP metric additionally averages ten IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95 in 0.05 increments. AP@0.50 is less strict about localization than AP@0.75. Inspect false positives, missed objects, sizes, and individual classes.

questions.stem: What should a team validate before deploying a real-time object detector on cameras or edge devices with changing lighting and crowded scenes?
options: Before deployment, test the detector on real cameras for latency, memory, power use, and object accuracy. Include dark and crowded scenes, check false alarms and missed detections, and monitor changes after release.

Test the detector's frame rate and memory use on a development computer, then assume it will behave the same on actual cameras. Check accuracy only on clean daytime examples because lighting changes are mostly a camera calibration problem.

Measure overall mAP and average inference time on clear test images to certify deployment readiness. If these two metrics are strong, crowded scenes, intermittent frame delays, and mistakes on rare objects need no additional testing.

Test the detector on target hardware and varied lighting, then consider average latency enough to guarantee real-time behavior. The number of processed frames also reveals localization errors and false alarms, so those measurements need not be repeated.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Edge object detection must meet timing and reliability requirements under realistic conditions. Evaluate p95 latency, memory, energy, and per-class recall on the target device; test small, crowded, partly hidden, and poorly lit objects. If a camera frame is resized or letterboxed, map predicted boxes back to original coordinates correctly. Quantization can reduce resources but should be re-evaluated for accuracy. For example, a warehouse safety camera needs false-alarm and missed-person audits, privacy controls, drift monitoring, and rollback.
